# Exploring the bioactive potential of green synthesized silver nanoparticles coated serratiopeptidase and chalcone derivatives

## 论文信息
- **期刊**: Discover Nano (2026)

## PMC 全文

**PMC ID**: PMC13263362

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and 
### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and 
### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and mosquitocidal capabilities Ajitha et al. [ 2 , 11 , 40 , 48 , 50 ]. Phyllanthus niruri , a member of the Phyllanthus family, has been used for the synthesis of silver nanoparticles that demonstrated antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and mosquitocidal characteristics [ 4 , 18 ]. A recent work by Kotaru et al. [ 28 ] found that silver nanoparticles synthesised from Phyllanthus niruri had anti-diabetic properties as well [ 28 ].

### Sample collection
Phyllanthus niruri plants were gathered from Kottooli, Calicut, Kerala, India, which is located at 11.261233° N, 75.799849° E. Phyllanthus niruri is a commonly seen wild medicinal plant in this region. The collected plant sample was identified and confirmed as Phyllanthus niruri L. by Dr. Rajasekaran C., Professor and Taxonomist, Department of Biotechnology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, India. The herbarium of Phyllanthus niruri was submitted with Specimen No. VITMN029-1 The plant was first rinsed with tap water and then thoroughly cleaned using double distilled water. The leaves were separated, blanched and washed followed by shade drying of the sample in sunlight for 1 week. After being ground with a grinder, the dried leaves were stored in an airtight container [ 30 ]. Synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) from Phyllanthus niruri

### Characterization of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) was characterized through various techniques, including UV–Vis Spectroscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), to confirm and analyze their functionality, functional groups, and morphology.
UV–Visible spectroscopy analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
Initial characterization of the silver nanoparticles was conducted using a UV–Visible spectrophotometer. The transition of silver ions into nanoparticle form was detected through the analysis of UV–Visible spectroscopy of the solutions following the dilution of the sample with 70% ethanol. The spectroscopy of the silver nanoparticles was performed from 300 to 600 nm, utilizing ethanol as the blank [ 8 ]. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
FTIR analysis was done using Agilent Cary 630, FTIR Benchtop Systems for the silver nanoparticles to find biomolecules and the functional groups that are responsible for reducing and stabilizing them. The recorded spectra were drawn as a graph of transmittance (%) vs. wavenumber (cm –1 ) [ 46 ]. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles were examined using X-Ray Diffraction with a D8 Advance X-ray Diffractometer (Bruker, Karlsruhe, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany), a secondary technique employed to ascertain particle size by the analysis of diffraction peaks. The Scherer equation was employed to determine the size of silver nanoparticles [ 3 ] ie; D = K × λ ÷ β × Cosθ. Zeta potential and dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The surface electric charge of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were evaluated by examining the most stable particles during instances of electrostatic repulsion among them. The zeta potential of the nanoparticle was assessed using the Particle Metrix Zetaview-PMX 130-Mono laser, while the hydrodynamic d

### Synthesis of chalcone derivative
The chalcone derivatives VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS were prepared by using different methods. Usually, chalcone compound synthesis follows a condensation reaction. VIT-A3S 6 was prepared using 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 and 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 as reactants along with ethanol and NaOH. 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 was fixed as the starting compound. The reaction order followed by initial addition of 0.1 g acetophenone 1 followed by 5 mL ethanol, 0.052 g NaOH and finally 0.11 g 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 . The contents in the round bottom flask were kept in a magnetic stirrer for 24 h at room temperature with constant stirring. VIT-PAGS 7 was synthesized using two steps: the hydroxyl groups were protected first and the Claisen Schmidt condensation followed. Salicylaldehyde 3 (0.610 g) was first methylated using 2.12 g of methyl iodide 4 , with potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) serving as a catalyst and 2 ml of dimethylformamide (DMF) as the solvent. The reaction was conducted at ambient temperature for 1 h, yielding 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 . In the next phase, 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (200 mg) was combined with 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.180 g) in an Claisen Schmidt condensation reaction that used 0.1598 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as the base and 6-7 mL of ethanol as the solvent. The reaction mixture was stirred continuously for 18 h at ambient temperature. Thin layer chromatography (TLC) was conducted at 2–3 h intervals to verify product formation. After the formation of product, the mixture was worked up using equal amount of ethyl acetate, dil. HCl and water in separating funnel for about 3 times and the organic phase was then dried and further purified [ 16 ].
Claisen Schmidt condensation was carried out between 0.665 mmol 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (0.1 g) and 0.665 mmol 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.11 g) in the presence of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in ethanol as the solvent. The quantities and equivalence indicated that a 1:1 molar ratio o

### Secondary screening for proteolytic activity by azo-casein assay
The modified protocol of Oda &amp; Murao [ 35 ] was followed for determining the protease activity of enzyme as well chalcone. To 200µL of chalcone and enzyme respectively, 0.05 mL of azo casein was added followed by incubation at 45 °C for 20 min. The subsequent step involved the addition of 0.06 mL Trichloro acetic acid (TCA) to terminate the reaction, followed by incubation of the contents on ice for 10 min. The contents were subsequently centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant, 0.3 mL of FC reagent and 0.45 mL of Na 2 CO 3 were added, followed by incubation in the dark for 30 min. The optical density was then measured at 660 nm [ 35 ].
Purification of serratiopptidase from Bacillus siamensis by triple phase partitioning method
Fresh seed culture of Bacillus siamensis ( PP077310 ). (3%) was inoculated into tryptic soy broth and incubated for 28 h followed by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant obtained, ammonium sulphate of 30% and equal volume of t-butanol was added. The contents were then kept in shaking incubator for 28 h at 37 °C [ 10 ]. Coating of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) to serratiopeptidase
Synthesised Ag NPs (10 g) along with 10 mL of purified enzyme is mixed with 10 mL of methanol and the contents were kept in magnetic stirrer for 4 h with constant stirring to evaporate the solvent. The remaining contents was collected and dried at 60 °C to obtain the nanoparticles coated enzyme. The silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated serratiopeptidase was then characterised by zeta potential and DLS [ 52 ]. Anti-inflammatory activity
Anti-inflammatory assay was performed according to the protocol described in Joseph et al. [ 25 ]. Freshly obtained human blood (5 mL) from a volunteer who had not taken NSAIDs for two weeks prior to the experiment was combined with an equal volume of sterilized Alsever’s solution. After centrifugation of the blood at 3000 rpm for 10 min, the packed cells were rinsed three times with an iso salin

### UV–visible spectra analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The UV–Vis spectra of the synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) had an absorption peak at 410 nm, signifying the effective synthesis of nanoparticles. The detected peak at 410 nm indicated that the nanoparticles possess a reduced size and a uniform distribution. UV–Vis spectroscopy validated the effective production of silver nanoparticles utilizing diverse plant extracts (Fig. 1 ).

### FT-IR analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The FTIR spectrum of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) showed functional groups like C=O, –OH, –CH and –NH groups which were the main functional groups in silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and confirmed that the green synthesized nanoparticles were silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). A band around 3425 cm 1 is indicative of O–H stretching, signifying the presence of polyphenols and flavonoids. The peaks at around 1653 cm 1 and 1510 cm 1 were the stretching vibrations of C=O and N–H groups indicating amide I and II, respectively. The spectral findings indicated that the main functional groups present in the plant extract played a dual role stabilizing the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and acting as capping agents (Fig. 2 ).

### XRD analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
There were distinct peaks obtained at specific 2θ values by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, corresponding to crystal planes (111, 200, 220, etc.), indicating the crystalline nature of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from Phyllanthus niruri . Specifically, peaks observed at 2θ angles of 38.06°, 44.23°, and 67.43° were attributed to (111), (200), and (220) planes, respectively, confirming the crystallinity of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 27 ] (Fig. 3 ).

### Zeta potential and DLS of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated Serratiopeptidase
Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and zeta potential analysis were used to characterize the Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation to evaluate changes in particle size and surface charge after enzyme interaction. Zeta potential revealed a mean value of − 32.28 mV, suggesting colloidal stability and a negatively charged nanoparticle surface. The formulation’s nanoscale size was confirmed by DLS analysis, which showed an average hydrodynamic diameter of about 50 nm. Serratiopeptidase coating with silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) is partially demonstrated by the observed changes in surface charge and particle size (Fig. 4 ).

### SEM Analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles predominantly exhibited a spherical morphology. The EDS spectrum showed the presence of Ag nanoparticle and the peak formed near 3 keV confirmed the formation of Ag and organic components like chlorine. It also revealed that the silver nanoparticles were in metallic form and free from impurities as the peak was maximum at the silver region which is 3 keV (Figs. 5 and 6 ).
Scanning electron microscopic (SEM) image of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) Fig. 6.

### Synthesis and purification of the chalcone compound
Both the chalcones VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 were synthesized using Claisen-Schmidt condensation using 5-methyl 2-hydroxy acetophenone 1 and different benzaldehydes. The detailed synthetic procedure and purification was given in Sect. 2.4 . The synthesized chalcones were then purified and characterized using different spectroscopic techniques including FT-IR, NMR and HPLC (Fig. 7 ).

### NMR analysis of chalcones
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-A3S 6 revealed 18 protons as well as 18 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 6 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.7 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 7.89 and 6.90 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 7.87 and 7.50 ppm. The protons of the methoxy groups appeared as 3H singlets at 3.97 and 3.94 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl carbon appeared at 193.6 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 110.6 ppm. The methoxy carbons resonated at 56.2 and 56.1 ppm. The peak at 20.8 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure.
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-PAGS 7 revealed 17 protons and 16 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 7 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.8 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 8.26 and 6.92 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 8.23 and 7.73 ppm. The protons of the methoxy group appeared as 3H singlet at 3.93 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7, the carbonyl carbon appeared at 194.2 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 111.4 ppm. The methoxy carbon resonated at 55.7 ppm. The peak at 20.7 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure (Fig. 8 ).
1 H NMR spectrum of chalcone VIT-A3S, b
1 H NMR expansion of chalcone VIT-A3S c
13 C NMR spectrum of chalcone VIT-A3S, d

### FTIR analysis of chalcones
In FT-IR analysis of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl functional group appeared at 1602 cm −1 . The FT-IR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7 confirms the presence of carbonyl functional group at 1640 cm −1 . In both the FT-IR spectra, the hydroxyl group in the spectrum is not appearing due to the intramolecular hydrogen bonding, where the carbonyl functional group is present adjacent to the hydroxyl group (Fig. 9 ).

### High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis of chalcone
The purity of both the chalcones were confirmed using HPLC. The HPLC spectra of VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 showed the percentage area of the compound to be 99.97% and 97.42% (Fig. 10 and Table 1 ).
HPLC chromatogram of chalcone a VIT-A3S and b VIT-PAGS Table 1.
HPLC data of chalcone VITA3S and VIT PAGS

### Purification of serratiopeptidase from Bacillus siamensis by TPP Method
Three distinct layers were observed in the solution after 24 h of incubation. The purified serratiopeptidase was found in the middle in the form of a white matte layer. The interfacial precipitate was found in between the aqueous phase in the lower region and the organic t-butanol layer in the upper region.
Proteolytic screening for chalcone
An apparent zone of hydrolysis was observed around wells containing chalcone derivatives at varying concentrations after 24 h of incubation on skim milk agar. The maximum zone diameter of around 20 mm was observed at the lowest concentration (1%) of chalcone in both VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS, whereas the higher concentrations showed reduced zones (Fig. 11 ).
a Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-A3S b Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-PAGS Proteolytic assay using azo-casein
The azo-casein assay performed with chalcone derivative alone showed an activity of 231.63 ± 0.43 U/mL and 228.77 ± 0.87 U/mL for VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS respectively at lower chalcone concentrations compared to higher concentrations (Fig. 12 ).
Activity observed in protein-based assays at different concentrations of chalcone derivatives a VIT-A3S and b VIT-PAGS. Groups not sharing a common letter are significantly different ( p &lt; 0.05) Anti-inflammatory activity
The percentage of protection of different concentrations of chalcones((VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS) are shown in Fig. 13 a, b. The values indicated that the chalcones have significant anti-inflammatory activity, inhibiting upto 92.67 ± 0.48%(VIT-A3S) and 91.99 ± 0.28%(VIT-PAGS) of inflammation in the assay, indicating its potential as a therapeutic agent. In addition the percentage of protection by silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated serratiopptidase was found to be 89.94 ± 0.06% and that of reference standard was 94.84 ± 0.31%.

### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s zeta potential investigation showed a negative surface charge of around − 32.28 mV, which is within the reported stability range for silver nanoparticles. Anandalakshmi et al. [ 5 ] similarly linked negative zeta potential values to increased colloidal stability of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), whereas David et al. [ 14 ] reported a zeta potential value of − 20.9 mV for green synthesised silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), attributing the negative charge of the capping by plant-derived polyphenols.

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and 
### Discussion

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and mosquitocidal capabilities Ajitha et al. [ 2 , 11 , 40 , 48 , 50 ]. Phyllanthus niruri , a member of the Phyllanthus family, has been used for the synthesis of silver nanoparticles that demonstrated antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and mosquitocidal characteristics [ 4 , 18 ]. A recent work by Kotaru et al. [ 28 ] found that silver nanoparticles synthesised from Phyllanthus niruri had anti-diabetic properties as well [ 28 ].

### Sample collection
Phyllanthus niruri plants were gathered from Kottooli, Calicut, Kerala, India, which is located at 11.261233° N, 75.799849° E. Phyllanthus niruri is a commonly seen wild medicinal plant in this region. The collected plant sample was identified and confirmed as Phyllanthus niruri L. by Dr. Rajasekaran C., Professor and Taxonomist, Department of Biotechnology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, India. The herbarium of Phyllanthus niruri was submitted with Specimen No. VITMN029-1 The plant was first rinsed with tap water and then thoroughly cleaned using double distilled water. The leaves were separated, blanched and washed followed by shade drying of the sample in sunlight for 1 week. After being ground with a grinder, the dried leaves were stored in an airtight container [ 30 ]. Synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) from Phyllanthus niruri

### Characterization of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) was characterized through various techniques, including UV–Vis Spectroscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), to confirm and analyze their functionality, functional groups, and morphology.
UV–Visible spectroscopy analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
Initial characterization of the silver nanoparticles was conducted using a UV–Visible spectrophotometer. The transition of silver ions into nanoparticle form was detected through the analysis of UV–Visible spectroscopy of the solutions following the dilution of the sample with 70% ethanol. The spectroscopy of the silver nanoparticles was performed from 300 to 600 nm, utilizing ethanol as the blank [ 8 ]. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
FTIR analysis was done using Agilent Cary 630, FTIR Benchtop Systems for the silver nanoparticles to find biomolecules and the functional groups that are responsible for reducing and stabilizing them. The recorded spectra were drawn as a graph of transmittance (%) vs. wavenumber (cm –1 ) [ 46 ]. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles were examined using X-Ray Diffraction with a D8 Advance X-ray Diffractometer (Bruker, Karlsruhe, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany), a secondary technique employed to ascertain particle size by the analysis of diffraction peaks. The Scherer equation was employed to determine the size of silver nanoparticles [ 3 ] ie; D = K × λ ÷ β × Cosθ. Zeta potential and dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The surface electric charge of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were evaluated by examining the most stable particles during instances of electrostatic repulsion among them. The zeta potential of the nanoparticle was assessed using the Particle Metrix Zetaview-PMX 130-Mono laser, while the hydrodynamic d

### Synthesis of chalcone derivative
The chalcone derivatives VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS were prepared by using different methods. Usually, chalcone compound synthesis follows a condensation reaction. VIT-A3S 6 was prepared using 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 and 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 as reactants along with ethanol and NaOH. 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 was fixed as the starting compound. The reaction order followed by initial addition of 0.1 g acetophenone 1 followed by 5 mL ethanol, 0.052 g NaOH and finally 0.11 g 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 . The contents in the round bottom flask were kept in a magnetic stirrer for 24 h at room temperature with constant stirring. VIT-PAGS 7 was synthesized using two steps: the hydroxyl groups were protected first and the Claisen Schmidt condensation followed. Salicylaldehyde 3 (0.610 g) was first methylated using 2.12 g of methyl iodide 4 , with potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) serving as a catalyst and 2 ml of dimethylformamide (DMF) as the solvent. The reaction was conducted at ambient temperature for 1 h, yielding 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 . In the next phase, 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (200 mg) was combined with 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.180 g) in an Claisen Schmidt condensation reaction that used 0.1598 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as the base and 6-7 mL of ethanol as the solvent. The reaction mixture was stirred continuously for 18 h at ambient temperature. Thin layer chromatography (TLC) was conducted at 2–3 h intervals to verify product formation. After the formation of product, the mixture was worked up using equal amount of ethyl acetate, dil. HCl and water in separating funnel for about 3 times and the organic phase was then dried and further purified [ 16 ].
Claisen Schmidt condensation was carried out between 0.665 mmol 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (0.1 g) and 0.665 mmol 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.11 g) in the presence of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in ethanol as the solvent. The quantities and equivalence indicated that a 1:1 molar ratio o

### Secondary screening for proteolytic activity by azo-casein assay
The modified protocol of Oda &amp; Murao [ 35 ] was followed for determining the protease activity of enzyme as well chalcone. To 200µL of chalcone and enzyme respectively, 0.05 mL of azo casein was added followed by incubation at 45 °C for 20 min. The subsequent step involved the addition of 0.06 mL Trichloro acetic acid (TCA) to terminate the reaction, followed by incubation of the contents on ice for 10 min. The contents were subsequently centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant, 0.3 mL of FC reagent and 0.45 mL of Na 2 CO 3 were added, followed by incubation in the dark for 30 min. The optical density was then measured at 660 nm [ 35 ].
Purification of serratiopptidase from Bacillus siamensis by triple phase partitioning method
Fresh seed culture of Bacillus siamensis ( PP077310 ). (3%) was inoculated into tryptic soy broth and incubated for 28 h followed by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant obtained, ammonium sulphate of 30% and equal volume of t-butanol was added. The contents were then kept in shaking incubator for 28 h at 37 °C [ 10 ]. Coating of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) to serratiopeptidase
Synthesised Ag NPs (10 g) along with 10 mL of purified enzyme is mixed with 10 mL of methanol and the contents were kept in magnetic stirrer for 4 h with constant stirring to evaporate the solvent. The remaining contents was collected and dried at 60 °C to obtain the nanoparticles coated enzyme. The silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated serratiopeptidase was then characterised by zeta potential and DLS [ 52 ]. Anti-inflammatory activity
Anti-inflammatory assay was performed according to the protocol described in Joseph et al. [ 25 ]. Freshly obtained human blood (5 mL) from a volunteer who had not taken NSAIDs for two weeks prior to the experiment was combined with an equal volume of sterilized Alsever’s solution. After centrifugation of the blood at 3000 rpm for 10 min, the packed cells were rinsed three times with an iso salin

### UV–visible spectra analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The UV–Vis spectra of the synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) had an absorption peak at 410 nm, signifying the effective synthesis of nanoparticles. The detected peak at 410 nm indicated that the nanoparticles possess a reduced size and a uniform distribution. UV–Vis spectroscopy validated the effective production of silver nanoparticles utilizing diverse plant extracts (Fig. 1 ).

### FT-IR analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The FTIR spectrum of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) showed functional groups like C=O, –OH, –CH and –NH groups which were the main functional groups in silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and confirmed that the green synthesized nanoparticles were silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). A band around 3425 cm 1 is indicative of O–H stretching, signifying the presence of polyphenols and flavonoids. The peaks at around 1653 cm 1 and 1510 cm 1 were the stretching vibrations of C=O and N–H groups indicating amide I and II, respectively. The spectral findings indicated that the main functional groups present in the plant extract played a dual role stabilizing the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and acting as capping agents (Fig. 2 ).

### XRD analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
There were distinct peaks obtained at specific 2θ values by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, corresponding to crystal planes (111, 200, 220, etc.), indicating the crystalline nature of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from Phyllanthus niruri . Specifically, peaks observed at 2θ angles of 38.06°, 44.23°, and 67.43° were attributed to (111), (200), and (220) planes, respectively, confirming the crystallinity of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 27 ] (Fig. 3 ).

### Zeta potential and DLS of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated Serratiopeptidase
Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and zeta potential analysis were used to characterize the Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation to evaluate changes in particle size and surface charge after enzyme interaction. Zeta potential revealed a mean value of − 32.28 mV, suggesting colloidal stability and a negatively charged nanoparticle surface. The formulation’s nanoscale size was confirmed by DLS analysis, which showed an average hydrodynamic diameter of about 50 nm. Serratiopeptidase coating with silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) is partially demonstrated by the observed changes in surface charge and particle size (Fig. 4 ).

### SEM Analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles predominantly exhibited a spherical morphology. The EDS spectrum showed the presence of Ag nanoparticle and the peak formed near 3 keV confirmed the formation of Ag and organic components like chlorine. It also revealed that the silver nanoparticles were in metallic form and free from impurities as the peak was maximum at the silver region which is 3 keV (Figs. 5 and 6 ).
Scanning electron microscopic (SEM) image of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) Fig. 6.

### Synthesis and purification of the chalcone compound
Both the chalcones VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 were synthesized using Claisen-Schmidt condensation using 5-methyl 2-hydroxy acetophenone 1 and different benzaldehydes. The detailed synthetic procedure and purification was given in Sect. 2.4 . The synthesized chalcones were then purified and characterized using different spectroscopic techniques including FT-IR, NMR and HPLC (Fig. 7 ).

### NMR analysis of chalcones
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-A3S 6 revealed 18 protons as well as 18 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 6 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.7 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 7.89 and 6.90 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 7.87 and 7.50 ppm. The protons of the methoxy groups appeared as 3H singlets at 3.97 and 3.94 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl carbon appeared at 193.6 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 110.6 ppm. The methoxy carbons resonated at 56.2 and 56.1 ppm. The peak at 20.8 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure.
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-PAGS 7 revealed 17 protons and 16 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 7 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.8 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 8.26 and 6.92 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 8.23 and 7.73 ppm. The protons of the methoxy group appeared as 3H singlet at 3.93 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7, the carbonyl carbon appeared at 194.2 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 111.4 ppm. The methoxy carbon resonated at 55.7 ppm. The peak at 20.7 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure (Fig. 8 ).

### FTIR analysis of chalcones
In FT-IR analysis of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl functional group appeared at 1602 cm −1 . The FT-IR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7 confirms the presence of carbonyl functional group at 1640 cm −1 . In both the FT-IR spectra, the hydroxyl group in the spectrum is not appearing due to the intramolecular hydrogen bonding, where the carbonyl functional group is present adjacent to the hydroxyl group (Fig. 9 ).

### High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis of chalcone
The purity of both the chalcones were confirmed using HPLC. The HPLC spectra of VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 showed the percentage area of the compound to be 99.97% and 97.42% (Fig. 10 and Table 1 ).

### Purification of serratiopeptidase from Bacillus siamensis by TPP Method
Three distinct layers were observed in the solution after 24 h of incubation. The purified serratiopeptidase was found in the middle in the form of a white matte layer. The interfacial precipitate was found in between the aqueous phase in the lower region and the organic t-butanol layer in the upper region.
Proteolytic screening for chalcone
An apparent zone of hydrolysis was observed around wells containing chalcone derivatives at varying concentrations after 24 h of incubation on skim milk agar. The maximum zone diameter of around 20 mm was observed at the lowest concentration (1%) of chalcone in both VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS, whereas the higher concentrations showed reduced zones (Fig. 11 ).
a Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-A3S b Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-PAGS Proteolytic assay using azo-casein
The azo-casein assay performed with chalcone derivative alone showed an activity of 231.63 ± 0.43 U/mL and 228.77 ± 0.87 U/mL for VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS respectively at lower chalcone concentrations compared to higher concentrations (Fig. 12 ).

The percentage of protection of different concentrations of chalcones((VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS) are shown in Fig. 13 a, b. The values indicated that the chalcones have significant anti-inflammatory activity, inhibiting upto 92.67 ± 0.48%(VIT-A3S) and 91.99 ± 0.28%(VIT-PAGS) of inflammation in the assay, indicating its potential as a therapeutic agent. In addition the percentage of protection by silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated serratiopptidase was found to be 89.94 ± 0.06% and that of reference standard was 94.84 ± 0.31%.

### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s zeta potential investigation showed a negative surface charge of around − 32.28 mV, which is within the reported stability range for silver nanoparticles. Anandalakshmi et al. [ 5 ] similarly linked negative zeta potential values to increased colloidal stability of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), whereas David et al. [ 14 ] reported a zeta potential value of − 20.9 mV for green synthesised silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), attributing the negative charge of the capping by plant-derived polyphenols.

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and 
### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s

### Introduction
Serratiopeptidase is a zinc-containing metalloprotease with a molecular weight between 45 and 60 kDa [ 23 ]. It possesses an extensive background in medicine and is commonly utilized to address various inflammatory conditions and inflammation. This enzyme has employed across various fields, including gynecology, orthopedics, surgery, dentistry and otorhinolaryngology due to its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiedema characteristics [ 51 ]. It is also reported for its proteolytic and fibrinolytic effects which are achieved by dissolving complement and enhancing plasmin activity through the inhibition of plasmin in-activators [ 7 ]. Organisms such as Serratia liquifaciens , Bacillus licheniformis , and Bacillus subtilis have also been documented for their synthesis of the enzyme serrapeptase. The advancement in nanotechnology and several studies demonstrated the efficacy and potential ability of silver nanoparticles in having anti-inflammatory properties [ 56 ]. There are several other nanoparticles reported to have anti-inflammatory property viz, Gold (Au), Zinc oxide (ZnO), Selenium (Se) etc. and the widely studied are the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 1 ]. Various species of Phyllanthus have been documented for the manufacture of silver nanoparticles. Phyllanthus emblica , Phyllanthus amarus , Phyllanthus pinnatus , and Phyllanthus urinaria L. are extensively utilized for the green synthesis of silver nanoparticles, which possess notable antibacterial, catalytic, and mosquitocidal capabilities Ajitha et al. [ 2 , 11 , 40 , 48 , 50 ]. Phyllanthus niruri , a member of the Phyllanthus family, has been used for the synthesis of silver nanoparticles that demonstrated antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and mosquitocidal characteristics [ 4 , 18 ]. A recent work by Kotaru et al. [ 28 ] found that silver nanoparticles synthesised from Phyllanthus niruri had anti-diabetic properties as well [ 28 ].

### Sample collection
Phyllanthus niruri plants were gathered from Kottooli, Calicut, Kerala, India, which is located at 11.261233° N, 75.799849° E. Phyllanthus niruri is a commonly seen wild medicinal plant in this region. The collected plant sample was identified and confirmed as Phyllanthus niruri L. by Dr. Rajasekaran C., Professor and Taxonomist, Department of Biotechnology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, India. The herbarium of Phyllanthus niruri was submitted with Specimen No. VITMN029-1 The plant was first rinsed with tap water and then thoroughly cleaned using double distilled water. The leaves were separated, blanched and washed followed by shade drying of the sample in sunlight for 1 week. After being ground with a grinder, the dried leaves were stored in an airtight container [ 30 ]. Synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) from Phyllanthus niruri

### Characterization of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) was characterized through various techniques, including UV–Vis Spectroscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), to confirm and analyze their functionality, functional groups, and morphology.
UV–Visible spectroscopy analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
Initial characterization of the silver nanoparticles was conducted using a UV–Visible spectrophotometer. The transition of silver ions into nanoparticle form was detected through the analysis of UV–Visible spectroscopy of the solutions following the dilution of the sample with 70% ethanol. The spectroscopy of the silver nanoparticles was performed from 300 to 600 nm, utilizing ethanol as the blank [ 8 ]. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
FTIR analysis was done using Agilent Cary 630, FTIR Benchtop Systems for the silver nanoparticles to find biomolecules and the functional groups that are responsible for reducing and stabilizing them. The recorded spectra were drawn as a graph of transmittance (%) vs. wavenumber (cm –1 ) [ 46 ]. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles were examined using X-Ray Diffraction with a D8 Advance X-ray Diffractometer (Bruker, Karlsruhe, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany), a secondary technique employed to ascertain particle size by the analysis of diffraction peaks. The Scherer equation was employed to determine the size of silver nanoparticles [ 3 ] ie; D = K × λ ÷ β × Cosθ. Zeta potential and dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The surface electric charge of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were evaluated by examining the most stable particles during instances of electrostatic repulsion among them. The zeta potential of the nanoparticle was assessed using the Particle Metrix Zetaview-PMX 130-Mono laser, while the hydrodynamic d

### Synthesis of chalcone derivative
The chalcone derivatives VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS were prepared by using different methods. Usually, chalcone compound synthesis follows a condensation reaction. VIT-A3S 6 was prepared using 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 and 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 as reactants along with ethanol and NaOH. 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 was fixed as the starting compound. The reaction order followed by initial addition of 0.1 g acetophenone 1 followed by 5 mL ethanol, 0.052 g NaOH and finally 0.11 g 3,4-dimethyoxy benzaldehyde 2 . The contents in the round bottom flask were kept in a magnetic stirrer for 24 h at room temperature with constant stirring. VIT-PAGS 7 was synthesized using two steps: the hydroxyl groups were protected first and the Claisen Schmidt condensation followed. Salicylaldehyde 3 (0.610 g) was first methylated using 2.12 g of methyl iodide 4 , with potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) serving as a catalyst and 2 ml of dimethylformamide (DMF) as the solvent. The reaction was conducted at ambient temperature for 1 h, yielding 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 . In the next phase, 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (200 mg) was combined with 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.180 g) in an Claisen Schmidt condensation reaction that used 0.1598 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as the base and 6-7 mL of ethanol as the solvent. The reaction mixture was stirred continuously for 18 h at ambient temperature. Thin layer chromatography (TLC) was conducted at 2–3 h intervals to verify product formation. After the formation of product, the mixture was worked up using equal amount of ethyl acetate, dil. HCl and water in separating funnel for about 3 times and the organic phase was then dried and further purified [ 16 ].
Claisen Schmidt condensation was carried out between 0.665 mmol 5-methyl-2-hydroxyacetophenone 1 (0.1 g) and 0.665 mmol 2-methoxybenzaldehyde 5 (0.11 g) in the presence of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in ethanol as the solvent. The quantities and equivalence indicated that a 1:1 molar ratio o

### Secondary screening for proteolytic activity by azo-casein assay
The modified protocol of Oda &amp; Murao [ 35 ] was followed for determining the protease activity of enzyme as well chalcone. To 200µL of chalcone and enzyme respectively, 0.05 mL of azo casein was added followed by incubation at 45 °C for 20 min. The subsequent step involved the addition of 0.06 mL Trichloro acetic acid (TCA) to terminate the reaction, followed by incubation of the contents on ice for 10 min. The contents were subsequently centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant, 0.3 mL of FC reagent and 0.45 mL of Na 2 CO 3 were added, followed by incubation in the dark for 30 min. The optical density was then measured at 660 nm [ 35 ].
Purification of serratiopptidase from Bacillus siamensis by triple phase partitioning method
Fresh seed culture of Bacillus siamensis ( PP077310 ). (3%) was inoculated into tryptic soy broth and incubated for 28 h followed by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 20 min. To the supernatant obtained, ammonium sulphate of 30% and equal volume of t-butanol was added. The contents were then kept in shaking incubator for 28 h at 37 °C [ 10 ]. Coating of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) to serratiopeptidase
Synthesised Ag NPs (10 g) along with 10 mL of purified enzyme is mixed with 10 mL of methanol and the contents were kept in magnetic stirrer for 4 h with constant stirring to evaporate the solvent. The remaining contents was collected and dried at 60 °C to obtain the nanoparticles coated enzyme. The silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated serratiopeptidase was then characterised by zeta potential and DLS [ 52 ]. Anti-inflammatory activity
Anti-inflammatory assay was performed according to the protocol described in Joseph et al. [ 25 ]. Freshly obtained human blood (5 mL) from a volunteer who had not taken NSAIDs for two weeks prior to the experiment was combined with an equal volume of sterilized Alsever’s solution. After centrifugation of the blood at 3000 rpm for 10 min, the packed cells were rinsed three times with an iso salin

### UV–visible spectra analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The UV–Vis spectra of the synthesized silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) had an absorption peak at 410 nm, signifying the effective synthesis of nanoparticles. The detected peak at 410 nm indicated that the nanoparticles possess a reduced size and a uniform distribution. UV–Vis spectroscopy validated the effective production of silver nanoparticles utilizing diverse plant extracts (Fig. 1 ).

### FT-IR analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The FTIR spectrum of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) showed functional groups like C=O, –OH, –CH and –NH groups which were the main functional groups in silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and confirmed that the green synthesized nanoparticles were silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). A band around 3425 cm 1 is indicative of O–H stretching, signifying the presence of polyphenols and flavonoids. The peaks at around 1653 cm 1 and 1510 cm 1 were the stretching vibrations of C=O and N–H groups indicating amide I and II, respectively. The spectral findings indicated that the main functional groups present in the plant extract played a dual role stabilizing the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) and acting as capping agents (Fig. 2 ).

### XRD analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
There were distinct peaks obtained at specific 2θ values by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, corresponding to crystal planes (111, 200, 220, etc.), indicating the crystalline nature of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from Phyllanthus niruri . Specifically, peaks observed at 2θ angles of 38.06°, 44.23°, and 67.43° were attributed to (111), (200), and (220) planes, respectively, confirming the crystallinity of the silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) [ 27 ] (Fig. 3 ).

### Zeta potential and DLS of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated Serratiopeptidase
Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and zeta potential analysis were used to characterize the Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation to evaluate changes in particle size and surface charge after enzyme interaction. Zeta potential revealed a mean value of − 32.28 mV, suggesting colloidal stability and a negatively charged nanoparticle surface. The formulation’s nanoscale size was confirmed by DLS analysis, which showed an average hydrodynamic diameter of about 50 nm. Serratiopeptidase coating with silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) is partially demonstrated by the observed changes in surface charge and particle size (Fig. 4 ).

### SEM Analysis of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs)
The synthesized nanoparticles predominantly exhibited a spherical morphology. The EDS spectrum showed the presence of Ag nanoparticle and the peak formed near 3 keV confirmed the formation of Ag and organic components like chlorine. It also revealed that the silver nanoparticles were in metallic form and free from impurities as the peak was maximum at the silver region which is 3 keV (Figs. 5 and 6 ).
Scanning electron microscopic (SEM) image of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) Fig. 6.

### Synthesis and purification of the chalcone compound
Both the chalcones VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 were synthesized using Claisen-Schmidt condensation using 5-methyl 2-hydroxy acetophenone 1 and different benzaldehydes. The detailed synthetic procedure and purification was given in Sect. 2.4 . The synthesized chalcones were then purified and characterized using different spectroscopic techniques including FT-IR, NMR and HPLC (Fig. 7 ).

### NMR analysis of chalcones
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-A3S 6 revealed 18 protons as well as 18 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 6 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.7 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 7.89 and 6.90 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 7.87 and 7.50 ppm. The protons of the methoxy groups appeared as 3H singlets at 3.97 and 3.94 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl carbon appeared at 193.6 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 110.6 ppm. The methoxy carbons resonated at 56.2 and 56.1 ppm. The peak at 20.8 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure.
The 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR analysis of the VIT-PAGS 7 revealed 17 protons and 16 carbon molecules. In 1 H NMR spectrum of compound 7 , the hydroxyl hydrogen appeared at 12.8 ppm. The aromatic protons resonated between 8.26 and 6.92 ppm. The olefinic protons of the double bond resonated as 1H doublets at 8.23 and 7.73 ppm. The protons of the methoxy group appeared as 3H singlet at 3.93 ppm. The protons of the methyl group in the structure resonated at 2.35 ppm as 3H singlet. In 13 C NMR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7, the carbonyl carbon appeared at 194.2 ppm. The aromatic carbons resonated in the range of 161.6 and 111.4 ppm. The methoxy carbon resonated at 55.7 ppm. The peak at 20.7 ppm corresponds to the methyl carbon in the structure (Fig. 8 ).

### FTIR analysis of chalcones
In FT-IR analysis of VIT-A3S 6 , the carbonyl functional group appeared at 1602 cm −1 . The FT-IR spectrum of VIT-PAGS 7 confirms the presence of carbonyl functional group at 1640 cm −1 . In both the FT-IR spectra, the hydroxyl group in the spectrum is not appearing due to the intramolecular hydrogen bonding, where the carbonyl functional group is present adjacent to the hydroxyl group (Fig. 9 ).

### High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis of chalcone
The purity of both the chalcones were confirmed using HPLC. The HPLC spectra of VIT-A3S 6 and VIT-PAGS 7 showed the percentage area of the compound to be 99.97% and 97.42% (Fig. 10 and Table 1 ).

### Purification of serratiopeptidase from Bacillus siamensis by TPP Method
Three distinct layers were observed in the solution after 24 h of incubation. The purified serratiopeptidase was found in the middle in the form of a white matte layer. The interfacial precipitate was found in between the aqueous phase in the lower region and the organic t-butanol layer in the upper region.
Proteolytic screening for chalcone
An apparent zone of hydrolysis was observed around wells containing chalcone derivatives at varying concentrations after 24 h of incubation on skim milk agar. The maximum zone diameter of around 20 mm was observed at the lowest concentration (1%) of chalcone in both VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS, whereas the higher concentrations showed reduced zones (Fig. 11 ).
a Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-A3S b Zone of hydrolysis of VIT-PAGS Proteolytic assay using azo-casein
The azo-casein assay performed with chalcone derivative alone showed an activity of 231.63 ± 0.43 U/mL and 228.77 ± 0.87 U/mL for VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS respectively at lower chalcone concentrations compared to higher concentrations (Fig. 12 ).
Activity observed in protein-based assays at different concentrations of chalcone derivatives a VIT-A3S and b VIT-PAGS. Groups not sharing a common letter are significantly different ( p &lt; 0.05) Anti-inflammatory activity
The percentage of protection of different concentrations of chalcones((VIT-A3S and VIT-PAGS) are shown in Fig. 13 a, b. The values indicated that the chalcones have significant anti-inflammatory activity, inhibiting upto 92.67 ± 0.48%(VIT-A3S) and 91.99 ± 0.28%(VIT-PAGS) of inflammation in the assay, indicating its potential as a therapeutic agent. In addition the percentage of protection by silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) coated serratiopptidase was found to be 89.94 ± 0.06% and that of reference standard was 94.84 ± 0.31%.

### Discussion
Nanoparticles generated from Hevea brasiliensis displayed a distinct absorption peak at 435 nm, signifying surface plasmon resonance, whereas a reduction in AgNO 3 concentration led to decreased particle sizes. Correspondingly, nanoparticles derived from Mangosteen leaves exhibited a peak absorption at 438 nm, characterised by good resolution and rapid scanning.
The extract of Jatropha curcas seeds was utilised to synthesise silver nanoparticles, exhibiting a notable absorbance peak at 425 nm [ 20 ]. Rajendrachari et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that the absorption peak at 435 nm is associated with electronic transitions between valence and conduction bands, hence affirming the production of silver nanoparticles.
In FTIR analysis, Haris et al. [ 22 ] observed absorption peaks at 2924, 3417, 1411, 1642, 1031, and 774 cm − 1 corresponds to similar functional groups and confirmed the presence of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs). According to Kumar et al. [ 29 ] silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) synthesized from leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri showed functional groups like C=O, –OH and C=N which validateed and confirmed the synthesised nanoparticles were silver. David et al. [ 14 ] revealed in his study that the XRD spectrum displayed four distinct Bragg's peaks at 2θ values of approximately 38.2°, 44.3°, 62.2°, and 77.9°. These peaks corresponded to the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of silver: {111}, {200}, {220}, and {311}, respectively. The Ag NPs-serratiopeptidase formulation’s zeta potential investigation showed a negative surface charge of around − 32.28 mV, which is within the reported stability range for silver nanoparticles. Anandalakshmi et al. [ 5 ] similarly linked negative zeta potential values to increased colloidal stability of silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), whereas David et al. [ 14 ] reported a zeta potential value of − 20.9 mV for green synthesised silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs), attributing the negative charge of the capping by plant-derived polyphenols.
